           PURA § 39.170(b)
     TEXAS-NEW MEXICO POWER COMPANY'S COMMENTS TO COMMISSION
       STAFF'S OUESTIONS FOR COMMENT ON DRAFT NEW 16 TAC § 25.521

TO THE HONORABLE PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS:

         Texas-New Mexico Power Company ("TNMP") respectfully submits these comments to

the Public Utility Commission of Texas ("Commission") in response to the Commission Staff' s

questions for public comment filed on July 24,2026, related to Rulemaking to Implement Large

Load Demand Management Service Under PURA §39.170. TNMP appreciates the opportunity to

submit these responses to questions and looks forward to collaborating with Commission Staff on

thi s proj ect.

                             I.      General Comments on Proposed Rule

         TNMP's comments address three issues that must be resolved before the rule is adopted.

First, the rule should confirm that the utility providing retail delivery service to the large load

customer must have, and must control, the facilities necessary to curtail that load during firm load

shed. Second, the rule must not permit one distribution service provider' s ("DSP") firm load shed

obligation to be satisfied through the curtailment of load served by a different DSP. Third, and

most consequentially, megawatts ("MW") procured and deployed as Large Load Demand

Management Service ("LLDMS") must be removed from the serving DSP' s firm load shed

obligation. Absent that correction, the same MW will be counted twice; once by ERCOT as a pre-

firm-load-shed demand reduction, and again by the DSP as load available to interrupt after ERCOT

declares Energy Emergency Alert ("EEA") Level 3. Only one ofthose calculations can be correct,




                                                 1
 and the resulting shortfall would fall on the DSP' s remaining customers, including residential

customers.
         A. The serving utility must have and control the facilities necessary to curtail the load

during firm load shed.

         PURA § 39.170(a) directs the Commission to require ERCOT to ensure that each electric

cooperative, transmission and distribution utility, and municipally owned utility serving a

transmission-voltage customer develops a protocol, "including the installation of any necessary

equipment or technology before the customer is interconnected," to allow the load to be curtailed

during firm load shed. The statute assigns that obligation to the utility that serves the customer,

which is the utility that provides retail delivery service at the customer' s location. 1 Proposed §

25.521(a)(1) tracks the statute.

         The proposed rule does not, however, state what the protocol must accomplish. Firm load

shed is an obligation ERCOT places on the transmission and distribution utility, and the utility is

the entity ERCOT and the Commission hold accountable for producing the directed MW. A

protocol that leaves the physical means of curtailment in the hands of the customer, a qualified

scheduling entity ("QSE"), or an entity operating behind the customer's meter does not satisfy the

statute, because the utility bearing the obligation would have no ability to discharge it. TNMP

recommends language requiring the protocol to give the serving utility the facilities, equipment,

and operational control necessary to curtail the load, and prohibiting assignment of that

responsibility to a third party.




116 TAC § 25.5(33) defines a distribution service provider to include an entity that distributes electricity to "retail
customers including retail customers served at transmission voltage levels.



                                                            2
          B. A DSP's firm load shed obligation cannot be assigned to, or satisfied by, another

DSP.

         For the same reason, the rule must not be read to permit a DSP' s firm load shed obligation

to be discharged by the curtailment of load that takes retail delivery service from a different DSP.

         1. There is no market rule or mechanism to reassign a firm load shed obligation.

         ERCOT allocates firm load shed obligations to transmission and distribution utilities by

load ratio share and issues instructions to each utility for its own system. No ERCOT protocol,

settlement construct, or accounting mechanism exists by which the curtailment performed by one

utility can be credited against the obligation of another. A rule that assumes a reallocation is

possible would create an obligation that cannot be measured, verified, or enforced, and would

leave both utilities uncertain as to what each is required to shed during an EEA Level 3 event

which is the moment when certainty matters most. TNMP recommends express language

foreclosing such reassignment.

         2. The obligation to interrupt retail load arises from the serving utility's tariff.

         A utility' s authority and obligation to interrupt a retail customer' s load arise from its

Commission-approved retail delivery tariff. Under 16 TAC § 25.241(b), a utility may not impose

any practice or regulation different from that prescribed in its effective tariff.2 That tariff

relationship serves two protective functions. It gives the customer notice, on Commission-

approved terms, of the circumstances under which its service may be interrupted; and it establishes

that the utility's interruption ofthat customer is performed in discharge of a tariff obligation rather

than as a discretionary act. A utility that interrupts load not taking service under its tariffhas neither




216 TAC § 25.241(b) ("No utility shall directly or indirectly... collect any rate or charge, or impose any...
practice or regulation different from that which is prescribed in its effective tariff filed with the commission.").



                                                            3
 the obligation nor that protection, and the affected customer has no tariff relationship through

which to understand or contest the interruption.

        C. MW procured as LLDMS must be excluded from the serving DSP's firm load shed

obligation.

        1. The proposed rule counts the same megawatts twice.

        Under proposed § 25.521(d) and (e), ERCOT procures LLDMS in advance of, or during,

an EEA event, deploys the large load customer on at least 24 hours' notice, and requires that

customer to remain deployed for the duration of the EEA event or until it can be safely recalled. If

the event escalates to EEA Level 3, ERCOT will direct firm load shed and allocate the required

MW among transmission and distribution utilities by load ratio share. At that point, the LLDMS

customer is already curtailed and is required by the rule to stay curtailed. Its load is not available

for the serving utility to shed.

        Nothing in the proposed rule removes those MW from the serving utility' s firm load shed

obligation. ERCOT is therefore relying on the same MW twice: once as a pre-EEA Level 3 demand

reduction procured under this section, and again as post-EEA Level 3 sheddable load embedded

in the utility's load ratio share. The load can only be there for one of them. One of the two

calculations is wrong, and the error is discovered only during an emergency.

        The Commission has already recognized this principle elsewhere in the proposed rule.

Proposed § 25.521(c)(2) makes a large load customer ineligible for LLDMS if it participates in

another reliability service, an ancillary service, an ERCOT-administered curtailment program, a

net metering arrangement that imposes a curtailment obligation under PURA § 39.169, firming

service, or a demand response product administered by a transmission and distribution service

provider. Those exclusions exi st because the same MW of demand reduction cannot be committed




                                                   4
 to two purposes at once. Firm load shed is the most consequential commitment of all, and the same

principle must apply to it. TNMP recommends a new § 25.521(j) excluding demand reduction

procured under the section and deployed, or subj ect to deployment, during an LLDMS obligation

period from the serving utility's firm load shed obligation for that period, and directing ERCOT

to conform its protocols and load shed allocation procedures.

       2. The shortfall is absorbed by the utility's remaining customers.

       The consequence is a shift in burden. If ERCOT directs a utility to shed a quantity of load

calculated on the assumption that the LLDMS customer' s demand is available, and that demand

has already been removed from the system under an ERCOT LLDMS deployment, the utility must

produce those MW, potentially several hundred MW or more for a single large load customer,

from its remaining customer base. Those customers are, overwhelmingly, commercial, and

residential customers. They would bear additional curtailment attributable to a service for which a

different customer is being compensated.

       3. The pool of interruptible load is shrinking, and the reliability risk is real.

       There is a question of whether the directed load shed can be performed at all. The quantity

ofload a utility may lawfully interrupt has contracted substantially since Winter Storm Uri. Critical

load industrial customers under PURA § 17.002 and critical natural gas facilities designated under

PURA § 38.074, the same categories the Commission has carved out of proposed §

25.521(a)(1)(A) and (B) have registered in significant numbers. A utility cannot interrupt those

loads through rotating outages; they come off the system only through under-frequency relay

operation, at which point the outcome is no longer controlled.

       During the February 2021 event, utilities had effectively exhausted their available load

shed capability. There were no remaining megawatts to drop. Adding LLDMS to the growing list




                                                  5
 of load that has been removed from the sheddable pool, while leaving the utility' s firm load shed

obligation unchanged, moves the system closer to the condition in which a utility is directed to

shed load it does not have. The failure mode in that scenario is an uncontrolled, system-wide outage

which is the precise outcome PURA § 39.170 was enacted to avoid.

       II.     Responses to the Commission's Questions for Comment

       A. Questions 1 through 3.

       TNMP takes no position at this time. TNMP reserves the right to address these questions

in reply comments.

       B. Question 4: Should ERCOT be allowed to deploy LLDMS for transmission

emergencies? If so, what limitations, if any, should the Commission impose on this authority?

       1. Yes, and the Commission should not impose artificial restrictions on when LLDMS

may be deployed.

       TNMP supports allowing ERCOT to deploy LLDMS during a transmission emergency,

and TNMP recommends more broadly that the Commission avoid narrow, categorical limits on

when the service may be called. ERCOT deploys ancillary services when doing so is operationally

and economically appropriate. LLDMS should be treated no differently. Where large load

customers are being compensated for a demand reduction obligation, ERCOT should be able to

call on that obligation as system conditions warrant.

       At a minimum, ERCOT should be required to deploy all procured and compensated

LLDMS capacity before directing firm load shed under EEA Level 3. Firm load shed is the last

resort in ERCOT' s emergency operating procedures. A resource that has been procured,

contracted, and paid for should not remain idle while firm customers, including residential

customers, are dropped.




                                                 6
        2. The proposed rule defines "transmission emergency" but never uses it.

       Proposed § 25.521(b)(4) defines "transmission emergency" as a condition in which an

element on the transmission system is operating above its emergency rating such that it creates a

significant risk of firm load shed. That defined term does not appear in any operative provision of

the rule. Proposed § 25.521(d) authorizes procurement only in connection with an EEA event due

to an extreme weather condition, and proposed § 25.521(e)(2) authorizes deployment only during

an EEA event due to an extreme weather condition. If the Commission intends to permit

deployment during transmission emergencies, subsections (d) and (e) must be revised to say so. If

not, the definition in subsection (b)(4) should be deleted to avoid ambiguity.

       3. Any expanded deployment authority must be paired with the exclusion described

in Section I.C.

       TNMP asks the Commission to adopt one limitation that goes hand in hand with broad

deployment authority. The more freely ERCOT may deploy LLDMS, the more often a large load

customer will be curtailed and unavailable to the serving utility at the moment firm load shed is

directed. Expanded deployment authority without the exclusion recommended in Section I. C

above would compound the double-counting problem. The two recommendations should be

adopted together.

       TNMP appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments and looks forward to

continuing to work with the Commission and Staff on these important issues.




                                                 7

      EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF TEXAS-NEW MEXICO POWER COMPANY'S
                            COMMENTS

       Texas-New Mexico Power Company ("TNMP") respectfully submits this executive

summary of its comments to the Public Utility Commission of Texas ("Commission") in response

to the proposal for publication filed on July 24,2026, related to the Rulemaking to Implement

Large Load Demand Management Service Under PURA § 39.170.


•      LLDMS megawatts must be excluded from the serving utility' s firm load shed obligation

       As drafted, the rule relies on the same MW twice: once as a pre-EEA Level 3 demand

       reduction procured by ERCOT, and again as post-EEA Level 3 sheddable load embedded

       in the transmission and distribution utility' s load ratio share. TNMP recommends a new §

       25.521(j) excluding demand reduction procured under the section and deployed, or subject

       to deployment, during an LLDMS obligation period from the serving utility' s firm load

       shed obligation for that period, and directing ERCOT to conform its protocols and load

       shed allocation procedures.


•      Without that exclusion, the shortfall is absorbed by the utility's remaining customers,

       including residential customers. A single large load customer may represent several

       hundred MW or more. If those MW remain in the utility' s obligation but are unavailable

       to shed, the utility must produce them from customers who are already being rotated

       through outages.



                                               9
 The consequence is a reliability risk, not merely a cost allocation issue. The pool of

interruptible load has contracted substantially since Winter Storm Uri as critical load

industrial customers, critical natural gas facilities, critical care and chronic condition

residential customers, and natural gas supply chain load have registered for protection.

During the February 2021 event, utilities had effectively exhausted their available load

shed capability. Assigning a utility an obligation larger than the load it can lawfully

interrupt risks an uncontrolled, system-wide outage - the outcome PURA § 39.170 was

enacted to prevent.


Proposed § 25.521(c)(2) already reflects the governing principle. The Commission has

made large load customers ineligible for LLDMS if they participate in another reliability

service, an ancillary service, a net metering curtailment arrangement under PURA §

39.169, firming service, or a utility demand response program, because the same MW

cannot be committed to two purposes at once. Firm load shed is the most consequential

commitment of all and must be treated the same way.


The utility providing retail delivery service must have and control the facilities necessary

to curtail the load. PURA § 39.170(a) assigns the protocol and equipment obligation to the

utility serving the transmission-voltage customer. A protocol that leaves the physical

means of curtailment with the customer, a QSE, or a behind-the-meter entity does not

satisfy the statute, because the utility that bears the firm load shed obligation could not

discharge it. TNMP recommends language requiring the protocol to give the serving utility

the facilities, equipment, and operational control necessary to curtail the load, and

prohibiting assignment of that responsibility to a third party. TNMP recommends language

requiring the protocol to give the serving utility the facilities, equipment, and operational

 control necessary to curtail the load, and prohibiting assignment of that responsibility to a

third party.


A DSP' s firm load shed obligation may not be satisfied by curtailment of load served by

another DSP. No ERCOT protocol or settlement mechanism credits one utility' s

curtailment against another utility' s obligation. Separately, the authority and obligation to

interrupt a retail customer arise from the serving utility' s Commission-approved tariff, and

under 16 TAC § 25.241(b) a utility may not impose practices outside its effective tariff.

That tariff relationship protects both the customer and the utility; a utility interrupting load

outside its tariff has neither the obligation nor that protection. TNMP recommends express

language foreclosing such reassignment.


Question 4: yes, and the Commission should avoid categorical limits on deployment

timing. ERCOT deploys ancillary services when doing so is operationally and

economically appropriate, and LLDMS should be treated no differently. At a minimum,

ERCOT must deploy all procured and compensated LLDMS capacity before directing firm

load shed under EEA Level 3; a resource that has been paid for should not sit idle while

firm customers, including residential customers, are dropped.


The rule defines "transmission emergency" in § 25.521(b)(4) but never uses it. Subsections

(d) and (e) authorize procurement and deployment only in connection with an EEA event

due to an extreme weather condition. If the Commission intends to permit deployment

during transmission emergencies, subsections (d) and (e) must be revised to say so.


Expanded deployment authority must be adopted together with the § 25.5210) exclusion.

The more freely ERCOT may deploy LLDMS, the more often the load will already be
